state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain why you think changing all the plant heights by the same proportion wouldn't affect the range?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, I think it's because like... if you cut them all in half, the difference between the biggest and smallest plant stays the same? Like the gap between them doesn't change even though the numbers get smaller. But I'm not really sure why adding the same amount to all of them would be different...

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of a situation where changing all the values by the same proportion would actually change the range?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher directly engages the misconception and maintains high cognitive demand, but the scaffolding in Turn 3 asks the student to find a counterexample when they've just revealed confusion about the core concept, and there's no evidence the student's understanding has improved by the dialogue's end.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher uses questions rather than direct answers, the question in Turn 3 actually contradicts the student's correct intuition (halving does change the range), which undermines rather than guides the student's reasoning through proper Socratic questioning.
